extracted.intended_audience: employers, industry stakeholders, economic analysts, small business representatives, and public commenters on OSHA's proposed heat standard
extracted.subtask_description: Economic-feasibility screening and related analytic methodology used by OSHA in the NPRM for a proposed heat standard, including thresholds, data adjustments, handling of missing data, and considerations for small/very small entities and market pass-through. Intended to support rulemaking and public comment on economic impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic feasibility screening tests (historical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency has historically used the two screening tests (costs less than one percent of revenue and costs less than ten percent of profit) as an initial indicator of economic feasibility; however, OSHA has discontinued use of the profit screening test because of its serious flaws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the cost-of-compliance <1% of revenue test as primary initial screen. Note: profit-based test (costs <10% of profit) was used historically but is no longer relied upon. If an industry exceeds the screening test(s), investigate further rather than treat it as dispositive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost-to-revenue threshold for feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Costs less than one percent of revenue is OSHA's primary screening threshold indicating the proposed standard is likely economically feasible for an industry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If average industry costs are below 1% of revenues (e.g., average for affected industries is 0.04%), OSHA treats compliance as feasible. If above 1%, OSHA identifies and discusses those industries and investigates further, and seeks public comment on practical effects and possible modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate screening for small and very small entities
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA examines average compliance costs per affected small entity and very small entity and relies on the same 1% of revenue screening test to evaluate impacts on small and very small entities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that small entities typically have higher average impacts due to diseconomies of scale; when small/very small entities exceed the threshold, OSHA will investigate further. The agency considers industry structure changes (e.g., closure of many small firms) as part of competitive-structure impacts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjustment of monetary data to base year
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA adjusted these figures to 2023 dollars using the BEA's GDP deflator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All cost and revenue figures should be converted to a common base year (2023) using the BEA GDP deflator to ensure comparability across datasets and years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling missing industry revenue data (QCEW to receipts conversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: For industries unavailable in SUSB (e.g., Rail 4821, Postal 4911, Insurance and Employee Benefit Funds 5251), OSHA used QCEW wage data and converted wages to annual receipts by applying the ratio of receipts to wages from the SUSB dataset for corresponding sector-level data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When receipts data are missing, convert reliable wage totals (QCEW) to receipts using sector-level receipts-to-wages ratios derived from SUSB. Document mappings and the sector-level ratios used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of compliance costs as variable vs fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: A large percentage of the costs of this proposed standard are variable costs because they depend primarily on the number and types of employees at an establishment. While fixed cost can be more limiting in terms of options for businesses, most of the costs of this standard are not fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize variable-cost nature in impacts analysis; variable costs are more easily scaled with output and may be passed through. Fixed costs can constrain options, but are less dominant here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market pass-through and output reduction dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: When an industry is subjected to a higher cost, it does not simply swallow it; it raises its price and reduces its output, and in this way shifts a part of the cost to its consumers and a part to its suppliers. Increases in prices in industries with elastic demand typically result in reduced quantity demanded, but rarely eliminate all demand for the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess ability to pass costs to customers (price increases) and expected reductions in output; consider demand elasticity and the likelihood that costs will be shared among consumers and suppliers rather than borne solely by firms. Use the quoted legal and economic reasoning (Am. Dental Ass'n v. Sec'y of Labor) as analytic precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situations that prevent cost pass-through
rubrics_metrics.description: Two situations typically mentioned when an industry subject to regulatory costs might be unable to pass those costs on: (1) foreign competition not subject to the regulation; or (2) domestic competition from other firms or other industries, not subject to the regulation, that produce goods or services that are close substitutes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate international and domestic competitive conditions. If significant foreign competition or unsubsidized domestic substitutes exist that are not covered by the standard, firms may be unable to raise prices to pass costs through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of broad applicability on competitive substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: When all establishments in an affected industry are covered by and required to comply with a standard, none of the competitors gain any economic advantage from the standard and the ability of a competitor to offer a substitute product or service at a lower price is greatly diminished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider scope of the standard (e.g., 29 CFR 1910.148's broad applicability) — broad coverage reduces potential for substitution to noncompliant competitors and supports greater pass-through capacity across the industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic-service industries and limited international competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Many employers that provide services affected by the proposed standard are generally not subject to international competition (e.g., personal services, such as child care, healthcare services and healthcare support services, and building support services like landscaping and maintenance) because they must be performed domestically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For services that must be produced locally, international competition is not a constraint on passing through costs; treat these industries differently in pass-through and feasibility assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of unquantified or hard-to-quantify benefits (cost offsets)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are more subtle benefits to reducing heat stress, which suggests that the actual net costs of the proposed standard will be lower than the cost estimates. These cost savings are difficult to quantify and include increased labor supply and decreased disutility to employees, increased retention, and wage cost offsets from increased productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and discuss potential non-monetized benefits (productivity gains, retention, reduced disutility) and consider them qualitatively or via sensitivity analysis; acknowledge they likely reduce net costs even if not fully quantified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of empirical examples to contextualize estimated impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA uses industry or program examples (e.g., Fair Food Program resulting in price increases of only one extra cent per pound of tomatoes) to suggest that robust protections may have small net price impacts in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate concrete programmatic or empirical examples to illustrate how compliance costs may translate to prices and consumer impacts; use such examples to question or refine modeled estimates when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of enforcement constraints in feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A longstanding appropriations rider generally prevents OSHA from enforcing its standards against most small farm operations with 10 or fewer employees, which affects likelihood of enforcement and thus how feasibility is evaluated for those industries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor legal/enforcement constraints (statutory riders, jurisdictional limits) into assessments of practical impacts and the likelihood of compliance/enforcement, particularly for sectors where OSHA lacks enforcement authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavioral or operational responses reducing exposure
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers could limit employees' time outside in high heat situations (e.g., to meet exemptions for short-duration employee exposure), which is a costless method to comply and could result in employers being exempt from the standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider non-costly operational changes (restricting outdoor work during extreme heat, using existing shade/shelter practices) as potential responses that reduce compliance burdens and affect impact calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigation and stakeholder input when thresholds exceeded
rubrics_metrics.description: In cases where industries (or small/very small entities) are above the threshold level for the primary screening test, OSHA will investigate further and welcomes public comment on likely practical effects and possible modifications to achieve greater feasibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When screening flags potential infeasibility, conduct deeper analysis and solicit targeted stakeholder input on practical effects and design modifications (e.g., exemptions, compliance flexibilities) to improve feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of industry turnover and organizational structure to assess output reduction options
rubrics_metrics.description: A reduction in output could happen in various ways (reduced service/production via reduced hours, marginal establishments closing, new entry delayed). The primary means depends on rate of turnover of establishments and on the form that the costs of the regulation take.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze industry structure (turnover rates, prevalence of marginal establishments, family-owned vs corporate composition) to predict which mechanisms (hours reductions, closures, delayed entry) are most likely to manifest if costs result in output reductions.
